Earth and Mars both orbit the Sun in the: Earth and Mars both orbit the Sun in the same direction. The line from Earth to Mars determines where Mars appears against distant stars.
Watch the changing line of sight in the: Watch the changing line of sight in the space view. Its apparent direction against the stars now moves westward: retrograde motion.
Earth passes between the Sun and Mars. M: Earth passes between the Sun and Mars. Mars is roughly opposite the Sun in our sky. Its orbit has not reversed.
Once Earth has passed, the line of sight: Once Earth has passed, the line of sight swings eastward again. The sky track records perspective, not a backwards orbit.
Half of Venus is illuminated by the Sun. From Earth we see only part of that illuminated hemisphere, depending on the angle between all three bodies.
Venus is well to one side of the Sun in: Venus is well to one side of the Sun in our sky. Its visible disc is close to half illuminated; the exact phase follows the actual geometry.
As Venus approaches the near side of its: As Venus approaches the near side of its orbit, its angular diameter grows while its illuminated fraction shrinks. The phase drawing is normalized in size so you can compare the shape.
After passing the Sun's direction, Venus: After passing the Sun's direction, Venus appears on its other side. The phase grows again. These diagrams are educational; use Observe's night-time guidance before aiming equipment.

Full Moon is an alignment in ecliptic lo: Full Moon is an alignment in ecliptic longitude. The Moon can still be above or below Earth's orbital plane, so it misses the shadow.
The lunar orbit is inclined by about fiv: The lunar orbit is inclined by about five degrees to the ecliptic. This small angle is enough to carry the Moon well clear of Earth's shadow at many full Moons.
In March 2025 the full Moon passes close: In March 2025 the full Moon passes close to the ecliptic plane and through Earth's shadow. Nodes are where the lunar orbit crosses that plane.
Crossing near the ecliptic alone is not: Crossing near the ecliptic alone is not enough. A lunar eclipse requires a full Moon and sufficiently close alignment with Earth's shadow. The normalized phase drawing does not simulate shadow darkening.
